content.title: Response to Reviewer v6pE
content.comment:
The motivation of the designed multimodal contrastive learning method is to obtain aligned multimodal representations towards the correct multimodal decisions. The current align-based methods align the paired modalities naively which may guide all unimodal representations to the wrong multimodal decisions. This paper introduces the positive, negative, and semi-positive pairs. The positive pairs are those samples with both correct unimodal decisions and are used to encourage getting closer unimodal representations for one positive pair. We argue that the sample with both wrong unimodal predictions is possibly difficult to get a correct decision. Compared with enlarging the similarity between two paired modalities with both wrong predictions, minimizing their similarity could get more different combinations of unimodal representations. We split these pairs into the negative category. For those samples with one correct unimodal prediction and one wrong unimodal prediction, we expect the unimodal representations could be aligned with the unimodal representations with accurate prediction. It means unimodal presentations with correct predictions are detached and have not been used for backward computing. 
The participating networks in our method are all tuned during training. The network of the baseline model is fixed or tuned are written already in Sec 4.2 in our paper.

Hard-sharing is a term in multi-task learning methods. As it has been explained in Sec 2.3, it means that the parameters are shared directly among different tasks. In our introduced multi-task learning framework, the parameters from the unimodal predicting task and the multimodal predicting task are also directly shared. I think the reviewer's interest may not so related to this topic and these terms are already described in the related work part of our paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6dsM
content.comment:
The multimodal classification task is not rale and actually, it is a much more general task. The datasets selected, such as Food-101, are also popular datasets for the multimodal classification task. I think the reviewer can find the used baseline methods on these datasets are all published in recent years’ mainstream conferences after the review read our paper more carefully (ME [1], Multimodal Dynamics [2], CF [3], TMC [4], etc., in Sec 4.2). The classification of each used modality is evaluated in each participating branch. It is not so meaningful to implement multimodal learning methods in the single-modality task, like image classification. I think the reviewer should read more related papers to get familiar with multimodal learning methods. 

This proposed method is proposed for the improvement of the aggregation-based method, and it is not so related to the reviewer’s proposed text-image retrieval task. Also, the reviewer mentioned ViLT method cannot achieve good results in this task, and we do not mention its performance in the submitted paper. We are considering adding it in the future version. 

Finally, we cannot agree that the multimodal classification task is not the mainstream task. The image classification task is a basic task in the computer vision area. However, I think not all methods are applicable to image classification though image classification is a common task. 

[1]: Liang, Tao, et al. "Expanding Large Pre-Trained Unimodal Models With Multimodal Information Injection for Image-Text Multimodal Classification." CVPR 2022.
[2]: Han, Zongbo, et al. "Multimodal Dynamics: Dynamical Fusion for Trustworthy Multimodal Classification." CVPR 2022.
[3]: Huang, Yu, et al. "What makes multi-modal learning better than single (provably)."NeurIPS 2021.
[4]: Han, Zongbo, et al. "Trusted Multi-View Classification." ICLR 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer VdyB
content.comment:
First, the assumption is verified in our ablation study. Thank you for your suggestions. We will provide more proof to justify this assumption. 

Second, the proposed multimodal contrastive method is based on the introduced multi-task-based methods and they work together to achieve the final performance. With the co-training of unimodal and multimodal predicting, we have obtained the unimodal representations for the initial alignment with the same target. Then the proposed multimodal contrastive loss further tunes the unimodal representation with the generated unimodal predictions and representations. 

The negative pair is penalized by the proposed multimodal contrastive loss. The cosine similarity is minimized when minimizing the contrastive loss. In this work, we do not add the weighing parameter for the positive and semi-positive pairs. The current setting has worked well and achieved our targets for aligning the unimodal representation towards the multimodal labels. Different modalities contribute differently to a multimodal task. We do not assume they contribute equally. The final multimodal representations from this proposed method are tuned based on each unimodal predicting result. The modality with a larger contribution will actually play a more important role in the proposed method. The unimodal representation from the inefficient modality is influenced by the representation with good prediction. When the work is finished completely, we will release our code and the details can be seen from the code for reference.

content.title: Response to Reviewer REcN
content.comment:
The motivation of the designed multimodal contrastive learning method is to obtain aligned multimodal representations towards the correct multimodal decisions. The current align-based methods align the paired modalities naively though providing a view for reducing the modality gap may guide all unimodal representations to the wrong multimodal decisions. 

This paper introduces the positive, negative, and semi-positive pairs for multimodal contrastive learning. The positive pairs are those samples with both correct unimodal decisions and are used to encourage getting closer to unimodal representations. We argue that the sample with both wrong unimodal predictions is possibly difficult to get a correct decision. Compared with enlarging the similarity between two paired modalities with both wrong predictions, minimizing their similarity could get more different combinations of unimodal representations to avoid overfitting for those “hard samples”. We split these pairs into the negative category. For those samples with one correct unimodal prediction and one wrong unimodal prediction, we expect the unimodal representations could be aligned with the unimodal representations with accurate prediction. It means unimodal presentations with correct predictions are detached and have not been used for backward computing. The assumption is evaluated in the ablation study in this paper. We will add further ablation studies in the future version.

The introduced framework is connected with the proposed multimodal contrastive loss. They two can be regarded as a whole. We get the unimodal predictions and unimodal representations from the multi-task framework. The proposed multimodal contrastive loss is based on them and is supervised by the unimodal training process.

To make it easier for every reader, we will further add detailed descriptions for the used abbreviations and notions. "UnsupMMC" and "SupMMC" are the commonly used unsupervised and supervised multimodal contrastive methods, respectively. “AGG" and "Early” are the aggregation-based method and early fusion methods in the multimodal learning area. We will make it easy to understand in the late version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper argues that naively combining unimodal representations may not be enough. They propose a framework where they (a) perform unimodal predictions, (b) look at the unimodal predictions and identify the agreement/disagreement in predictions (also wrt to ground truth), and (c) and use the agreement/disagreement between these predictions to align feature vectors from different modalities using contrastive loss.  Authors show through experiments in 4 data sets that their method is effective.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think the paper is clear and well written. I agree with the authors that better way to extract complimentary information from different modalities is an important and open problem. 

Overall, I think the framework introduced my authors by thinking in terms of the correctness of unimodal framework is interesting. However, I do not completely understand the rational behind some of the choices:
1. I agree that when both the unimodal predictions are correct, they are positive pairs are the representations should be close to each other. 
2. When both the unimodal predictions are wrong, the authors argue labelling them as negative pairs and push away their representations, so that  "to explore a larger possibility of correct prediction". This doesn't seem to be well justified. 
3. When one prediction is correct, and the other is not, the features from the incorrect prediction tends towards the features from correct prediction which is "frozen". Given that all components are trained together, is this necessary? Can authors provide ablation/justification for introducing this semi-correct category? 

I've troubling following the experiments section. For example,  Can the authors define what different abbreviations like "UnsupMMC" and "SupMMC" exactly mean in Table 1 (and their differences) - I tried searching for these terms in the paper, but couldn't get a hit in the main body. Similarly, what exactly does "AGG" "Early" mean? I think it's some kind of aggregation, but defining this would be useful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is reasonably clear (see above for an example). I think there's enough information to reproduce the experiments (Section A.2)
content.summary_of_the_review: I think, overall the paper is interesting and proposing a pretty good idea. However, some choices in the proposed framework needs justification, and the overall presentation of the paper needs be better (terms defined).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper improves multimodal representation learning quality by increasing the agreement among the unimodal representations with each other. The proposed approach first shared the unimodal representations for unimodal tasks and multimodal tasks. Then authors propose to use contrastive learning to align the unimodal tasks prediction consistency. The work is evaluated against multiple multimodal datasets and outperforms the SOTA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strength*
- The analysis and design for contrastive pair sampling strategy is somewhat novel.
- The extensive experiments are sufficient to validate the proposed approach

*Weaknesses*
- The proposal relies on a strong assumption that all unimodal predictions should agree with each other when designing the contrastive loss. But in my opinion, this assumption may not generally applicable. Authors can refer to any previous proof to justify this assumption.
- The proposed approach is limited to aggregation based multimodal learning due to its nature of parameter sharing.
- From Table 4, though the UniS-MMC yield the best performance, the majority performance gain is already observed in MT-MML. In another word, the gain mainly comes from the parameter sharing and co-training unimodal and multimodal together which diminishes the contribution of contrastive loss which is the most novel part of this paper. Obviously, authors tried to justify the contribution of contrastive loss in Figure 4 and table 5, but the gains from MT-MML to UniS-MMC are still marginally significant
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- 1: Not sure if I missed anything, but how do you penalize Negative pair in L_mmc? Please clarify
- 2: In equation 5, should you consider positive pair and semi-positive pair has different contribution by adding some weighing parameter?
- 3: different modalities may contribute differently, assuming they contribute equally may not be optimal.
- 4: Do you consider use contrastive design to align multimodal prediction and unimodal prediction for any modality?
- 5: [writing comment] It might not be necessary to over use notations and too detailed descriptions to denote common knowledges nowadays like cross-entropy, log-loss, etc in section 3.1,3.2, can be more succinct.
content.summary_of_the_review: The writing is clear and the experiments are sufficient. The novelty is limited as 1) parameter sharing is intuitive 2) contrastive loss contribution is not as significant as expected.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a multi-task-based multimodal learning framework by sharing between the multimodal learning branch and the unimodal learning branches. It also propose a novel multimodal contrastive method based on unimodal predictions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
(a) The multi-task-based multimodal learning framework combines the benefits of both multimodal learnign and multi-task learning, which is novel to me.
(b) The experiments show the strength over some existing baselines in different tasks and datasets.
Weaknesses
(a) The method choose some very rare tasks such as food classification, news classification and medical-related classification tasks, did not evaluate on any mainstream uni-modality tasks (e.g. image classification) and cross-modality tasks, (e.g. text-image retrieval, Visual Question Answering), thus preventing us from comparing with other self-supervised learning baselines. The author should consider including using similar setting covered in Table 3, 4, 5 of ViLT [1].

[1]  Vilt: Vision-and-language transformer without convolution or region supervision, ICML 2021

content.title: UniS-MMC: Learning Unimodality-supervised Multimodal Contrastive Representations
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel multi-task-based multimodal contrastive method for multimodal representation learning (multimodal classification task).
content.abstract:
Multimodal learning aims to imitate human beings to acquire complementary information from multiple modalities for final decisions.  
However, just like a human's final decision can be confused by specific erroneous information from the environment, current multimodal learning methods also suffer from uncertain unimodal prediction when learning multimodal representations. In this work, we propose to contrastively explore reliable representations and increase the agreement among the unimodal representations that alone make potentially correct predictions.
Specifically, we first capture task-related representations by directly sharing representations between unimodal and multimodal learning tasks. With the unimodal representations and predictions from the multitask-based framework, we then propose a novel multimodal contrastive learning method to align the representations towards the relatively more reliable modality under the weak supervision of the unimodal predictions.
Experimental results on two image-text benchmarks UPMC-Food-101 and N24News, and two medical benchmarks ROSMAP and BRCA, show that our proposed Unimodality-supervised Multimodal Contrastive (UniS-MMC) learning method outperforms current state-of-the-art multimodal learning methods. The detailed ablation studies further demonstrate the advantage of our proposed method.
